title: Portrait and Verdict
premise: When the coffin of town founder Edmund Harrow is exhumed for a centennial ceremony, coroner Ansel Okafor finds it empty—and the replacement body inside is a man everyone believed died fifteen years ago, the night Ansel filed his death certificate. As Ansel investigates, he realizes the killer is someone who has read every file he ever sealed: someone from the town's inner circle using old records to stage a reckoning for crimes the founders buried. The trail leads to Harrow's living descendants and to Ansel's own complicity in the original cover-up. In the end, Ansel traps the killer in the archive itself, but chooses to expose the truth—including his own signature on the false papers—trading his invisibility for a justice the law never delivered.
about_author: Ines Yarrow is the pen name of a former small-town records clerk who spent a decade cataloguing deaths in rural municipal archives before turning to fiction. She writes mysteries about paper trails, quiet towns, and the people who know too much to stay silent.

chapters.title: The Weight of Names
chapters.summary: Ansel Okafor's POV. We meet him tending the cemetery he knows grave by grave, establishing his ritualized invisibility and pride in order. The centennial committee orders Edmund Harrow's exhumation for a ceremonial reburial. Emotional beat: contentment shadowed by unease—he remembers what's written in that particular file.

chapters.title: Empty Oak
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. The coffin is opened before witnesses: no founder, only the body of Daniel Voss, declared dead fifteen years ago on paperwork bearing Ansel's own signature. Panic ripples through the crowd. Emotional beat: vertigo—his carefully alphabetized world cracking open in public.

chapters.title: Fifteen Years of Paper
chapters.summary: Ansel privately re-reads his old files at night, confirming Voss's certificate was falsified under pressure from then-mayor Ruth Calloway. He tells no one. Emotional beat: guilt resurfacing like water in a flooded basement.

chapters.title: The Committee's Grief
chapters.summary: Deputy investigator Mara Quist's POV. She interviews the founding families—the Harrows, Calloways, and Ashfords—who close ranks with practiced smoothness. Mara notices they ask about Ansel more than about the body. Emotional beat: an outsider smelling rot beneath civic pride.

chapters.title: What Voss Knew
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Flashback to 2009: Voss, a young journalist, came asking about a drowned girl whose death was ruled accidental. Days later he vanished; Ansel signed the certificate he was handed. Emotional beat: shame hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: A Second Empty Grave
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Another founder-era grave is found opened overnight—also empty, with a typed index card left inside referencing a case number only the coroner's office would hold. Emotional beat: realization that the killer isn't taunting police; he's auditing Ansel.

chapters.title: The Man Who Filed Me
chapters.summary: Ansel receives a letter quoting his own marginalia verbatim, including notes he never entered into any official record. The writer invites him to 'complete the record.' Emotional beat: hunted intimacy—the killer knows his handwriting better than his friends do.

chapters.title: Calloway's Confession, Almost
chapters.summary: Ansel confronts aging Ruth Calloway, who admits Voss was silenced but insists she only arranged the paperwork, not the killing—and that someone else dictated the terms. She begs him to let the past stay filed. Emotional beat: pity tangled with fury.

chapters.title: Index of the Drowned
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. She pulls the drowned girl's file—Lily Ashford, 1998—and finds Ansel's mentor, the previous coroner, signed it. The old guard all touched it. Emotional beat: dawning scope of the conspiracy.

chapters.title: Night Shift
chapters.summary: Ansel stakes out the cemetery and catches a figure at the Harrow plot—but it's young Theo Harrow, the founder's great-grandson, leaving flowers and a case file page. Theo flees. Emotional beat: suspicion redirected, trust misplaced.

chapters.title: The Apprentice's Ledger
chapters.summary: Ansel discovers his late mentor's private ledger listing payments from the founding families—a parallel archive someone else has clearly been reading. A page is missing. Emotional beat: understanding that two people have been keeping score.

chapters.title: Quist Closes In
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. She matches the typewritten index cards to a discontinued model used by the county records annex—and finds the annex volunteer log suspiciously redacted. She begins suspecting someone inside her own circle of interviewees. Emotional beat: methodical hope.

chapters.title: Threat in Triplicate
chapters.summary: Ansel finds three copies of Voss's real autopsy report—never filed—slipped into his home, dated the week of the murder. The killer wants him to read it. Emotional beat: terror curdling into a terrible clarity: he's being recruited, not threatened.

chapters.title: Theo's Bargain
chapters.summary: Theo Harrow confesses to Ansel: he found the ledger years ago and blackmailed the families quietly, but someone stole his research and began killing. He names the annex volunteer: Walter Finch, the beloved town historian. Emotional beat: alliance formed out of mutual blackmail and genuine grief.

chapters.title: Finch's Museum
chapters.summary: Mara and Ansel search Finch's cottage: walls of clippings, timelines, photographs of every founding-family sin—except Finch denies everything, calmly, and his alibi for Voss's murder holds. Emotional beat: the floor dropping out—they've found a curator, not necessarily a killer.

chapters.title: The Missing Page
chapters.summary: Ansel reconstructs the torn ledger page from memory: it recorded a payment made fifteen years ago to a second man—the driver, the hands, not the mind. The name is one nobody suspects: the current mayor, David Ashford, Lily's uncle. Emotional beat: revulsion as the town's kindly face becomes its mask.

chapters.title: Ashford's Centennial
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mayor Ashford announces the reburial will proceed in three days, rushing past objections. Mara notices the ceremony's guest list includes every person connected to the old files. Emotional beat: dread—the killer is curating an audience.

chapters.title: Rehearsal for a Reckoning
chapters.summary: Ansel decodes the killer's letters as stage directions: the empty graves mirror the sequence of the original crimes, and the final 'exhibit' is scheduled for the reburial itself. He realizes he is meant to be the witness—or the final exhibit. Emotional beat: fear transmuted into strategy.

chapters.title: The Archive Trap
chapters.summary: Ansel feeds false information through Theo, luring the killer to the records annex at night by implying the ledger's last page proves Ashford acted alone. Mara waits in the dark stacks. Emotional beat: cold courage—the invisible man finally sets a snare.

chapters.title: Verdict in the Stacks
chapters.summary: Climax. The killer emerges—not Finch but his protégé, the annex clerk, Lily's childhood friend who watched every adult bury the truth. He forces Ansel to choose: burn the files or die with them. Ansel talks him down by offering something better than destruction: publication. Ashford is arrested as the clerk surrenders the evidence. Emotional beat: mercy chosen over vengeance.

chapters.title: Signature in Ink
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. At the hearing, he testifies to everything, including his own forged certificate, surrendering his license. The town turns on him and then, slowly, doesn't—because half of them were waiting for permission to grieve honestly. Emotional beat: exposure as a strange relief.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Ansel's POV. A year later he tends graves without a badge, Voss and Lily finally marked with true stones. Mara visits; the town is imperfectly, painfully honest now. He writes the last entry in his private ledger: not a death, but a correction. Emotional beat: belonging earned through truth rather than silence.
